headline: Zuckerberg's Bizarre War on Whistleblowers Escalates with Million-Dollar Fines
summary: Meta is reportedly using arbitration to silence former employee Sarah Wynn-Williams, fining her over $11 million for criticizing the company in her memoir.
details: More than a decade ago, Belarusian dissidents used whimsical protests like "ice cream socials" to challenge their authoritarian government, daring it to crack down on innocuous behavior.
This tactic revealed the regime's willingness to punish even the smallest actions, highlighting its paranoia and cruelty.
Now, a similar, albeit less whimsical, battle is unfolding in the UK, involving Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and a former whistleblower.

Sarah Wynn-Williams, author of the memoir "Careless People," details alleged criminality and severe personal failings within Facebook's executive team, including Mark Zuckerberg, Sheryl Sandberg, and Joel Kaplan.
The book reportedly touches on Meta's alleged encouragement of genocide in Myanmar and Zuckerberg's decision to grant China censorship powers.
Following the book's publication, Meta reportedly used an arbitration clause in Wynn-Williams's employment contract to silence her.
An arbitrator, paid by Meta, ordered her to never promote or speak about her book, imposing fines of $50,000 per criticism.
These fines have accumulated to over $11 million, a sum that reportedly exceeds Wynn-Williams's and her husband's total assets and lifetime earning potential.
caption:
Mark Zuckerberg is reportedly fining a whistleblower over $11 million for criticizing Meta in her memoir.

More than a decade ago, Belarusian dissidents used whimsical protests like "ice cream socials" to challenge their authoritarian government, daring it to crack down on innocuous behavior.

This tactic revealed the regime's willingness to punish even the smallest actions, highlighting its paranoia and cruelty.

Now, a similar, albeit less whimsical, battle is unfolding in the UK, involving Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and a former whistleblower.

Sarah Wynn-Williams, author of the memoir "Careless People," details alleged criminality and severe personal failings within Facebook's executive team, including Mark Zuckerberg, Sheryl Sandberg, and Joel Kaplan.

The book reportedly touches on Meta's alleged encouragement of genocide in Myanmar and Zuckerberg's decision to grant China censorship powers.

Following the book's publication, Meta reportedly used an arbitration clause in Wynn-Williams's employment contract to silence her.

An arbitrator, paid by Meta, ordered her to never promote or speak about her book, imposing fines of $50,000 per criticism.

These fines have accumulated to over $11 million, a sum that reportedly exceeds Wynn-Williams's and her husband's total assets and lifetime earning potential.

headline_marked: California bans [[streaming ads louder than content]] starting July 1
headline: California bans streaming ads louder than content starting July 1
summary: New law aims to bring ad volume parity between streaming services and traditional TV, following similar legislation in Illinois.
details: Starting July 1, 2025, California will prohibit streaming platforms from broadcasting commercial advertisements at a volume exceeding that of the accompanying video content. This move aligns streaming services with broadcast, cable, and satellite providers, which are already subject to the Commercial Advertisement Loudness Mitigation (CALM) Act.

The CALM Act, enforced by the FCC, requires that commercials maintain the same average volume as the programs they interrupt. While the exact implementation details for streaming services remain unclear, it is anticipated that companies may extend these volume adjustments to all US streams, not just those detected within California.

Illinois has also passed similar legislation, with its ad loudness requirements for streaming services set to take effect by July 1, 2027. This indicates a growing trend towards regulating ad volume across different media platforms.

Major industry groups, including the Motion Picture Association and the Streaming Innovation Alliance, reportedly opposed the California bill. Their concerns centered on the complexities of managing ad loudness, particularly with server-side ad insertion which can lead to inconsistencies due to various encoding pipelines.

These groups also highlighted the challenge of accommodating a wide range of user devices, from large TVs to small phones, each with different audio capabilities. The FCC has previously received thousands of complaints regarding ad loudness from viewers of traditional broadcast and cable services.
